messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am running a joint hurdle model looking at the occurrence of a fish species. I am trying to get yearly occurrence predictions using summary.fitted.values by referencing my prediction stack (with y=NA) however I'm not sure the code is correct. I am predicting to each mesh node and so call 1:n_mesh_nodes when running inla.mesh.project, this seems to work fine for year 1 but when I try to get predictions for the following year they are either the exact same, or make no sense. I was able to join a set of covariates to each mesh node using the nearest neighbour function and so obtain my new locations for predicting to (which matched the number of mesh nodes).

Example, with 400 mesh nodes I would use:

## get predictions for the prediction stack
index_pred <- inla.stack.index(joint.stack,"pred")$data
lp_sum<-test$summary.fitted.values$mean[index_pred]

## select the first n rows of predictions to match number of mesh nodes
lp_sum1<-as.data.frame(lp_sum)
lp_sum1= lp_sum1[1:400,]

u.proj<-inla.mesh.projector(q_mesh1)
m.proj<-inla.mesh.project(u.proj, lp_sum1)

and for the following year use lp_sum1= lp_sum1[401:800,]

Is this the correct way to obtain yearly predictions? Sample code and files attached.

Any help is greatly appreciated!

Thanks,

Paul

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA group

I have an irregular spatiotemporal lattice dataset. I would like to apply BYM models with Held’s four spatiotemporal interactions on my data.

I notice that the article “Scaling intrinsic Gaussian Markov random field priors in spatial modelling” and the Chapter 7 of the book “spatial and spatio-temporal bayesian models with r - inla” choose merely “rw1” and “rw2” as examples. On the contrary, when I try to code on INLA, I find that I can choose “ar1” models as well. Here is my code.

f13 <-  Sec_Res ~ count.nat+count.phy + household1 + old_rat1 + Mea500+littoral + int.rat+tax1 +

  f(ID.area, model="bym", graph=Corsica.adj.Q,adjust.for.con.comp = FALSE,constr = TRUE,scale.model = T) +

  f(Seq1,model="ar1") + f(Seq2,model="iid") +

  f(ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int>,model="iid", group=ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int>,control.group=list(model="ar1"))

Since the cases on the article and the book introduce “rw1” and “rw2” prior, I am not sure that whether replace “rw” prior by “ar” prior is possible?

Whether INLA produces correct and accurate results in “ar1” cases?

Many thanks

Charles

messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

To check your code in general, I suggest making up some known space-time surface, adding noise and seeing if you can recover said surface. Very small noise with fixed (known) variance (control.family=...).

Predicting to each mesh node depends on the structure of your formula. The space-time effects can be predicted by just extracting it at the mesh nodes in space-time, as you would do when plotting (before projection to a grid). The other effects in the predictor depend on how you want to interpolate them to the mesh nodes.

If you have all the space-time covariate information at the space-time mesh nodes, the NA trick you are doing might work. To do this you need NA for each mesh node at each time point! However, the NA trick in the space-time models have some stability issues, because you are adding #meshnodes*#years fake datapoints, and constructing the predictor based on posterior samples of each random and fixed effect may be safer.

To check that the $time covariate in the stack comes in the order you think that it does, you can do "(str(stack))" and investigate the object

You can also make two separate stacks for the first 2 years to be sure of the indexing, and compare it to what you are doing now. You can even fit two different models with the two different years' prediction stacks (using the same data fitting stack in each).

PS: I checked your code briefly, and nothing stood out to me as wrong.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.subject_clean: Issue with small number variable
messages.body_plain:
Hello list,

I am modelling the probability of recaptures from a mosquito MR experiment. My model has a binomial likelihood, default INLA priors and a spatio-temporal structure, here is my R code to run it:

outinla<-inla(pa ~ 1 + sex + dist ... + dayfromrel f(parid, model="bym2", graph=MAD.adj) + f(parid_g, dayfromrel, model = "iid",constr=TRUE) ,family="binomial",data=iso4m, Ntrials=daily_abundance,control.compute=list(waic = TRUE))

Now I want to transform "dist" variable (which represents the distance of recapture from release point) using a negative exponential kernel and use the transformed distance as a predictor. The literature on the topic suggests that this should improve model predictions.

The issue is that the transformed distance (range: 5.74e-08-1.14e-06) is 6-8 order of magnitude smaller than the other predictors and when I add it to the model, the posterior probability distribution for its model term does not make much sense, due to a huge standard deviation (mean=0.0136, sd=31.6228).

If I substitute the variable with a vector of 0's, the sd deviation of the posterior distribution remains the same.

Is there an explanation for this behaviour? How I can add this variable and obtain a reasonable estimate of its posterior distribution?

Thanks,
Matteo

messages.subject_clean: Using Pardiso to speed up computations on a Windows server with 32 cores
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I wanted to use the Pardiso library to speed up my computations. I am using INLA on a Windows server with 32 cores and 256 GB RAM. My models are usually very large with 1.6 individuals located in 1600 municipalities and take around a day to run. It is a logistic regression with 1.6 million lines as data input.

I followed the suggestions to obtain a Pardiso license. Here is the code I used:

inla.setOption("pardiso.license", "D:/Paradiso/pardiso.lic")

model <- inla(y~  1 +  x1+ x2  + x3+
                       x4+ x5 + x6+
                       f(idx.age, age, model = "rw2", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.001)))) +
                       f(area, model = "bym",
                         graph = "D:/INLA/total", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.001)))),
                     family = "binomial",  control.family = list(link = "logit"), data=data, control.compute = list(dic=T, openmp.strategy ="pardiso.parallel"),
                     control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb", reordering = "amdc"), verbose = T)

summary(model)

However, I noticed that there is no improvement in computation speed.

Is there anything else I have to do? I assume INLA already contains the components of Pardiso, so that I don`t have to install anything extra?

I am running INLA which I installed in May this  year.

Any help is greatly achieved.

Best, Boris

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm attempting to replicate the structure of a Stan model in INLA (Really looking forward to INLA's speed!)

This is a mixed effects model on score for individuals, each with repeated measures.  There are a few fixed and random effects.  I attempted fitting with all the priors left to default, but after 10 hours of running, and multiple warnings about Hessian problems, killed the process.  We have strong domain knowledge on this study, so it would make sense to manually tune some of the hyper-parameters/priors to help INLA. (i.e. the intercept should be around 11, and the random_effects should each be small, with mean 0 and maybe sd around 1)

While this is easy in Stan, I can't figure out how to do the same thing with INLA.

Here is the basic model.  Can anybody offer some guidance on how to adjust the hyper-parameters/priors for the random (group) effects?

subject_id2 <- subject_id
model_test <- inla(score ~ 1  + factor_1 + factor_2 + I(factor_2^2)
                        + f(rand_effect_1, model="iid")
                        + f(rand_effect_2, model="iid")
                        + f(subject_id, model="iid") + f(test_seq, replicate=subject_id2, model="ar1")
                       , data=df, family="gamma", control.compute=list(config = TRUE), verbose=TRUE)

# Note:  test_seq is in integer that increments for each subject when they take the test.  Can think of it as a measure of each subject's experience

I'm also not 100% sure the last line is correct.  My intent is to have a slope per-subject, and then an autoregressive term for each subject that is AR1 (Their score/ability evolves over time.)

Does this model look correct for the subject intercept and AR term?
How/where can I adjust the hyper-parameters / priors for the 4 random effects (rand_effect_1, rand_effect_2, subject_id, test_seq)

Thank You!

messages.body_plain:
A few tricks you can try:

## Priors
If you don't know what priors to use, use the pc priors, e.g.
hyper1 = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.01)))
formula1 = y ~ f(plate, model="iid", hyper=hyper1)
(see https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic106.html)

And similarly for the ar1 process (https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic117.html).

## Factors
I suggest coding all of the factors manually as 0-1 covariates (one for each factor level). Whether you remove the intercept or not depends on how you code the factors. The easiest way to be absolutely sure you know what is going on with factors is to do the manual work.

## Fixed effects
You can use control.fixed to set the priors for these.

## Logfile
Please attache the output of the verbose=T, or the fit$logfile in future emails.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Yes, you can specify such a model in several ways. When using spde models in inla, one tends to use inla.stack() constructions, and then one can include the covariate, vegetation in your case in the A matrix for evaluating the field.

There are three main cases:
1) the covariate is known at the observed points.
2) the covariate is known on a grid
3) the covariate is known on the mesh nodes

If one wants to do prediction, case 2 or 3 are required.

The suggestions below all use f(w, model=spde) in the inla formula, and introduce the covariate multiplication in the A matrix in an inla.stack() call.

In case 1, let A be the A matrix for evaluating the field on the mesh (please refer to the extensive case studies and examples on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org> for details on this.
Let veg be the vector of vegetation values for each observation.
Then you need to use
  Diagonal(length(veg), veg) %*% A
as the A matrix in the inla.stack call instead of just A.

In case 3, let veg be the vector of vegetation values for each mesh node.
Then you need to use
  A %*% Diagonal(length(veg), veg)
as the A matrix.

In case 2, in the past I’ve used a preprocessing step to map the covariate onto the mesh first, and then proceed as in case 3.
Nowadays I would use the inlabru interface instead, where one old define a function of the coordinates to evaluate the covariate at arbitrary locations, and construct the desired multiplication in the model formula, as
  veg(x,y) * field

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Here is some R code for messing with priors in a simple hierarchical regression model.

# some code for messing around with priors for simple hierarchical
# regression model. read "Spatial and Spatio-temporal Bayesian Models
# with R-INLA" for more info.

# set up
library(INLA)
library(inlabru)
library(brinla)
set.seed(123)

# start making data
m <- 1000 # sample size
set.seed(123)
x <- runif(m, 10, 50) # independent var
grp <- sample(seq(1, 10), size=m, replace=T) # groups

# simulate random intercept
tau.grp <- 0.01 # set precision
(sigma.grp <- sqrt(1/tau.grp)) # as standard deviation
set.seed(4455)
v <- rnorm(length(unique(grp)), 0, sqrt(1/tau.grp)) # random intercept
vj <- v[grp] # assign effect to individuals

# simulate y
tau.meas <- 0.04 # measurement error
(sigma.meas <- sqrt(1/tau.meas))
b0 <- 5 # intercept
beta1 <- 1.5 # slope
set.seed(334455)
y <- rnorm(m, b0 + vj + beta1*x, 1/sqrt(tau.meas)) # make response
dat1 <- data.frame(x, y, grp)

# plot it
ggplot(data=dat1, aes(x, y, col=factor(grp))) + geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm")

# define and run model with default priors, where prior for global intercept
# is norm(0, 0), global x effect is norm(0, 0.0001), and tau.grp is
# loggamma(1, 0.00005), I think.
form1 <- y ~ 1 + x + f(grp, model="iid")
out1 <- inla(form1, family="gaussian", data=dat1,
             control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive", # balance speed, precision
                               int.strategy="auto"),
             control.compute=list(config=T), # for posterior sampling
             num.threads=3, # control number threads
             verbose=T)
summary(out1); plot(out1)
bri.hyperpar.summary(out1)

# define and run model with specified priors, where prior for global intercept
# is norm(0, 0.01), global x effect is norm(0, 0.01), and tau.grp is pc.prior

Hello,

I'm attempting to build a model with some fixed and random effects.  However, the outcome variable is repeated for each subject, over time.  Plotting the subject's scores clearly indicates a different slope and intercept for each subject.

m <- lmer(score ~ f1 + f2 + (1+attempts|subject))

fm1 <- formula(score ~ f1 + f2 + f(subject, model="iid") + f(subject, attempts, model="ar1")

fm2 <- formula(score ~ f1 + f2 + f(subject, model="iid") + f(attempts, replicate=subject, model="ar1")

# From Faraway book
nid <- length(unique(subject))
subject2 <- subject + max(subject)
fm2 <- formula(score ~ f1 + f2 + f(subject, model="iid2d", n=2*nid) + f(subject2, attempts, copy="subject")

Some questions:
1) fm1 has two labels in the second f().  I don't know how INLA handles this, but is this a correct way to calculate a per-subject slope?
2) fm2 also seems to generate on random effect slope, for each subject, but is this better/different than fm1
3) fm3 comes directly from Faraway book.  However, I can't figure out how to make the per-subject slope have an autoregressive term.

Any thoughts or explanation would be greatly appreciated!!!!

Hi and thx for your email.

I'm not 100% sure about your model...

if you have subjects 1,2,3..., with covariates 'attempts' and you want
to coefficient for 'attempts' to have an AR1 structure, then its like

y ~  ... f(subject, model="iid") +
         f(time.subject, attempts, model="ar1", replicate = subject)

where 'time.subject' is the time-point within each subject. There are
some details here, that the the time-points are regular and complete,
otherwise you can give them through the arguments 'values'

y ~  ... f(subject, model="iid") +
         f(time.subject, attempts, model="ar1", replicate = subject,
           values = 1:10)

which will give you the time-points 1:10  and then 'time.subject' can
be one of them as it like.

the second argument 'attempts' is the covariate which scales the AR1
term. if that argument is missing, its defaults to 1.

I would use the pc.cor1 prior for the correlation in the AR1, as the
simpler model is that its constant, see the Stat.sci paper about
penalized complexity priors from last year.

let me know if you still have issues,

H

I think is better to change it in one of the two ways bellow

1. use constr=FALSE in

RESP~ f(ID.PM10, PM10, model="iid", graph=torino.adj, constr=FALSE, ...

2. add the overall coefficient
RESP~ PM10 + f(ID.PM10, PM10, model="iid", graph=torino.adj, constr=TRUE, ...

The first gives a regression coefficient for each area. The interpretation is as usual, just depending on the link function used for the linear predictor.

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] constrained refined Delaunay triangulation.
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
The “constrained” part is the least relevant; it just means that one can specify that certain polygons/line must be part of the triangulation edges. The only constrained edges are usually the boundary edges. The quality of the spde approximation depends mostly on the “refined” aspect. Meshes with small and well-formed triangles (short edges, and no small acute angles) provide closer approximations. Meshes with large and/or sharp angled triangles exhibit approximation artifacts; the fields are always conditionally deterministic, given the values at the mesh vertices. This, for example, shows up as a non-constant variance. See meshbuilder() in the INLA package for a tool to analyze this effect. (Turn on the mesh assessment checkbox)

Finn
